title: Palmer Penguins
text: This dataset comes from the TidyTuesday project (week of July 28, 2020). It includes body measurements for three species of penguins Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo that live on islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. title: Palmer Penguins
text:
Plot


Code
library(tidyverse)

penguins <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-07-28/penguins.csv')

penguins |>
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Flipper Length vs. Body Mass in Palmer Penguins",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Emily Dickinson’s Poems
text:
Emily Dickinson wrote short poems about broad subjects and used dashes frequently (--). I used string functions and regular expressions to ask:

Which themes (death, love, nature, God) show up most often in her poems?
Does her use of dashes differ across the three groups of poem files in the data?

title: Emily Dickinson’s Poems
text:
Data source
R package: DickinsonPoems by Nicholas Horton, available at https://github.com/Amherst-Statistics/DickinsonPoems and installed with devtools::install_github("Amherst-Statistics/DickinsonPoems"). Original source: the Project Gutenberg edition of Emily Dickinson’s poems, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/12242/12242-h/12242-h.htm. * Each poem is stored as its own text file (like gutenberg1.txt001). I call the digit after “gutenberg” the “file group” (1, 2, or 3).

title: Emily Dickinson’s Poems
text:
Read in the data
The regular expression (?<=gutenberg)\\d uses a lookbehind to grab the digit that comes right after “gutenberg” in the file name.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(DickinsonPoems)

poems <- tibble(file = list_poems()) |>
  mutate(
    text = map_chr(file, \(f) str_flatten(get_poem(f), collapse = "\n")),
    group = str_c("File group ", str_extract(file, "(?<=gutenberg)\\d")),
    n_dashes = str_count(text, "--")
  )

title: Project 2: Emily Dickinson’s Poems
text:
Clean the data
Each poem starts with a Roman numeral like XIX., then usually an ALL-CAPS title, then the poem itself. I use regular expressions to pull these pieces apart.

(?<=gutenberg)\\d is a lookbehind: it grabs the digit that comes right after the word “gutenberg” in the file name.
[IVXLC]+(?=\\.) is a lookahead: it grabs the Roman numeral only if a period follows it.
[^a-z\\n]*[A-Z][^a-z\\n]* matches a line with no lowercase letters (the title).



Code
poems <- poems_raw |>
  mutate(
    raw = str_trim(raw),
    group = str_extract(file, "(?<=gutenberg)\\d"),
    group = str_c("File group ", group),
    roman = str_extract(raw, "^[IVXLC]+(?=\\.)"),
    body = str_trim(str_remove(raw, "^[IVXLC]+\\.")),
    title = str_extract(body, "^[^a-z\\n]*[A-Z][^a-z\\n]*(?=\\n)"),
    text = str_trim(str_remove(body, "^[^a-z\\n]*[A-Z][^a-z\\n]*\\n")),
    n_dashes = str_count(text, "--")
  ) |>
  select(file, group, roman, title, text, n_dashes)

title: Project 2: Emily Dickinson’s Poems
section: Question 1: Which words does she use most?
text:
Question 1: Which words does she use most?
I pull out every word with the regular expression [a-z']+ (letters and apostrophes), then remove a short list of very common words so that the interesting words stand out.


Code
stop_words_small <- c("the", "and", "that", "with", "for", "was", "are", "but",
                      "not", "you", "all", "his", "her", "they", "this", "have",
                      "from", "will", "has", "had", "its", "were", "who", "when",
                      "then", "than", "there", "their", "she", "him", "our", "can",
                      "one", "would", "could", "what", "which", "upon", "thy",
                      "thee", "thou", "been", "into", "more", "does", "just")

all_words <- tibble(
  word = unlist(str_extract_all(str_to_lower(poems$text), "[a-z']+"))
)

top_words <- all_words |>
  filter(str_length(word) > 2, !word %in% stop_words_small) |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 12)

top_words

section: Question 2: How does her use of dashes compare across file groups?
text:
Question 2: How does her use of dashes compare across file groups?


Code
dash_by_group <- poems |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    poems = n(),
    avg_dashes = mean(n_dashes)
  ) |>
  mutate(group = fct_reorder(group, avg_dashes))

section: Bonus table: words right before a dash
text:
Bonus table: words right before a dash
A lookahead lets me grab the word before a -- without including the dash itself.

pre_dash <- tibble(
  word = unlist(str_extract_all(str_to_lower(poems$text), "[a-z']+(?=\\s*--)"))
) |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)

title: Emily Dickinson’s Poems
text:
Conclusion
Her poems return to a few big themes, and the dash is a regular part of her style. A limitation is that my keyword lists were chosen by hand, so they miss words I didn’t think of. The text for each poem also includes its title and number, which might add extra matches.

title: Emily Dickinson’s Poems
section: Question 1: Which themes show up most?
text:
Question 1: Which themes show up most?
For each theme I wrote a regular expression of related words. (?i) makes it ignore capital letters, and \\b marks a word boundary so that “die” can’t inside a longer word. str_detect() checks whether each poem contains a match, and the average of those TRUE/FALSE values is the share of poems with that theme.


Code
themes <- poems |>
  summarise(
    Death = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(death|die|dies|died|dying|dead|grave)\\b")),
    Love = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(love|loved|loves|lover)\\b")),
    Nature = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(bee|bees|bird|birds|flower|flowers|sun|snow|wind)\\b")),
    God = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(god|heaven|angel|angels|eternity)\\b"))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "theme", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(theme = fct_reorder(theme, share))

themes


# A tibble: 4 × 2
  theme   share
  <fct>   <dbl>
1 Death  0.215 
2 Love   0.0662
3 Nature 0.308 
4 God    0.194 




Code
ggplot(themes, aes(x = share, y = theme)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of Poems Mentioning Each Theme",
    subtitle = "Based on keyword matches",
    x = "Percent of poems with at least one matching word",
    y = "Theme"
  )









What the plot shows. Each bar is the percent of poems that contain at least one word from that theme, with the most common theme at the top. The most common theme is Nature, which appears in 31% of the poems. The least common is Love, at 7%. This is a rough measure, because a poem can use the word “grave” without being mainly about death.

  <fct>             <dbl>
1 File group 1      0.52 
2 File group 2      0.722
3 File group 3      0.828




Code
ggplot(dash_by_group, aes(x = group, y = avg_dashes)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Number of Dashes per Poem",
    subtitle = "Compared across the three file groups",
    x = "File group",
    y = "Average dashes per poem"
  )









What the plot shows. Each bar is the average number of dashes (--) per poem in one file group, ordered from lowest to highest. The group with the most dashes is File group 3, at about 0.8 per poem. The group with the fewest is File group 1, at about 0.5. If the bars are close, the dash is a steady habit across her poems, and if they differ a lot, the groups are quite different in style.
